Hanna,

That is way less complex than what you were asking before. You could do this with a join.

#translation table (AKA "lookup table") that is a table with 4 columns instead of lists
trans_table2 <-

tibble(
symb = c("S","Ls", "sL", "SCL","loam","SitL", "sC","cL","SiLc", "siC", "clay"),

sand = c(90,80,65,60,40,20,52.5,33.3,10,47,20),
silt = c(5,5,10,27.5,20,15,42.5,33.3,32.5,6,65),
clay = c(5,15,25,12.5,40,65,5,33.3,67.5,47,15)
)
# this is your input table. I changed L to loam. Your symbols/soiltypes need to be consistent! Please check them.
input_table <-
tibble(
Depth = c("0-33", "33-66", "66-100", "100-133", "133-166", "166-200"),
soil = c("siC","siC","siC","siC","loam","loam")
)

# now join from the translation table and only keep what exists in your input_table
dplyr::left_join(input_table, trans_table2, by = c("soil" = "symb"))
# "by" is important here since the names of our joining column do not match

# A tibble: 6 x 5
  Depth   soil   sand  silt  clay
  <chr>   <chr> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>

3 66-100  siC      47     6    47
4 100-133 siC      47     6    47
5 133-166 loam     40    20    40
6 166-200 loam     40    20    40

HTH,
B

library(zoo)
library(tidyverse)

df <- expand.grid(date1 = as.Date(c(1, 2, 5, 6)),
            site = c(1, 2)) %>%
  mutate(nitrate = rnorm(8)) %>%
  as_data_frame

## your function:
my_function <- function(x) {

  x <- zoo(x$nitrate, x$date1)

  x.new <http://x.new> <- zoo(NA, seq(min(time(x)), to =  max(time(x)),by="day"))
  x.new <http://x.new>[time(x)] <- x

  res <- na.approx(x.new <http://x.new>)
  data_frame(date = index(res),
             nitrate = as.numeric(res))

}

## test on 1
my_function(x=filter(df, site==1))

## apply to all
df %>%
  nest(-site) %>%
  mutate(new = map(data, my_function)) %>%
  unnest(new)

Hi Hanna,

1. Assuming you want your loop to load the files and combine them into one big dataframe, try something like
> files = list.files(data_dir)
> files_with_path = str_c(data_dir, files)
> dataf = map_dfr(files_with_path, read_csv, .id = ’sourcefile’)

This uses tidyverse packages.  map_dfr is a version of map (so takes the elements in the first argument and applies the function in the second argument) that combines the results into a single dataframe.  The .id argument adds a column corresponding to the item’s name in the list.

2. First, I’m assuming you have good reasons for thinking these are sensor failures and should be trimmed.  (You probably do, I just wouldn’t be a good DSI postdoc if I didn’t do some finger wagging about trimming data.)

>  - based on threshold values (larger than x is an outlier)
> - more than x standard deviations from the mean value
> - change in value or total variation over x seconds is greater than y
> - before the first x seconds
>
Some of these will work fairly differently from others in R.

messages.body_plain:
Hi

I am trying to write a fast function to do matrix group-wise centering: for each variable in the matrix, center the variable by removing the mean, yet the mean is to be calculated at the group level.

dplyr solution is waaay too slow, data.table seems much better, but still could benefit from some improvement ( I am very new to data.table). I wrote some benchmark code and posted on Stack Exchange - Code review, but had little feedback so far: https://codereview.stackexchange.com/questions/203513/group-wise-deviations-from-means-centering-with-dplyr-vs-data-table

If anyone has some good understanding of data.table, or want to throw an alternative (R base ?) solution, that would be greatly appreciated! You could get some virtual points on stack overflow, and a very real coffee on campus :-)

Everything is on the post, but for archiving purpose, here is in a nutshell the question. I found 2 data.table solutions:
- 1) compute for each variable the function x - mean(x), group-wise
- 2) add the mean variables in the data.table, then compute the difference between raw columns and mean columns

Intuitively, 1 should be way faster: we are not adding more variables in the data.table, and doing it in one operation. Yes in practice 2) is faster... why? I might not be using the full benefit of mean optimisation in data.table? How to write it as a anonymous function in the data.table way, instead of the classical way function(x) x - mean(x)

Thanks!!

Matthieu

messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

Thanks for adding me to the group. I am Ozias from the Swedish University of Agriculture in Uppsala. I am facing some issue with R and though I tried to trace the error online I could not solve the issue with the online answers.

In brief, I :
(1) I want to extract some digital elevation (dem) raster files from a bigger one based on3 different polygon shapefiles
(2) After extraction, I want to save the 3 raster files with the names e.g. demReg1, demReg2, demReg3 in my directory.
Because I am using a high resolution raster file, I prefer to run the code in parrallel using a foreach loop.
Here is my code below:

#Load Libraries
library(sp)
library(rgdal)
library(doParallel)#Foreach Parallel Adaptor
library(foreach)#Provides foreach looping construct

#Define how many cores to use
UseCores <- detectCores()

#Register CoreCluster
cl<- makeCluster(UseCores)
registerDoParallel(cl)

#Set working directory
setwd("..../Example")

#Load in the shapefile
reg1 <- readOGR('Reg1.shp')
reg2 <-readOGR('Reg2.shp')
reg3 <- readOGR('Reg3.shp')

#Create a list of shapefile
reg <- c(reg1,reg2,reg3)

#Use foreach loop and %dopar% command
foreach(i=1:length(reg)) %dopar% {
  library(raster)
  library(sp)
  library(rgdal)

  CRS<-CRS("+init=epsg:3006")
  spTransform(reg[[i]], CRS)

  r1<-raster("C:/Users/ozho0001/Documents/arc_gis_data/R_test/demtest.tif")

  dem.ext<-extract(r1, reg[[i]])

  f <- paste0('demReg', i, '.tif')

  writeRaster(dem.ext, filename=f)
}
#End Cluster
stopCluster(cl)

I got the following errors:   Error in { :
  task 1 failed - "unable to find an inherited method for function 'writeRaster' for signature '"list", "character"'".

I have attached a folder containing a very small raster file and shapefile to test the code above.

I will appreciate any help,

Best Regards,
Ozias

I suspect in your case what you mean by "extract" is covered by the crop() function: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/raster/versions/2.6-7/topics/crop

Note that the crop function can write directly the raster! This should save you a lot of effort (and lot of on-cache disk writing). The ... argument in crop() refer to arguments in writeRaster directly!

Matthieu

messages.body_plain:
Yes, these are all good pointers, but if you are using non-rectangular shapefile polygons as part of the process, here's something else to be aware of:

Mask will return a raster with the same extent as the original raster but with elevations converted to NA outside the shapefile polygon.

Crop will return a raster with an extent that the shapefile can fit into.  So, except for rectangular or square polygons used for cropping, you will still have elevations in your "cropped" raster that are actually outside of the polygon boundary.

I'm not sure what your end goal is, but it's possible you may want to do a crop (to reduce the extent and memory demands of the raster) followed by a mask (to have data only for your area of interest).

Scott

Hi all!

I am trying to add the labels for significant differences between combinations of two factors, and am having some difficulties.

When I have one factor with any number of levels, my code works fine.
For example (where test5 is my glmm, and SamplePer is the factor of interest):

SamplePer = lsmeans(test5, ~ SamplePer)
SamplePer = cld(SamplePer, alpha=0.10, Letters=letters, adjust="tukey")

Which gives an object of type 'summary_emm' and 'data.frame' looking like this:

                      levels=c("Jan","Feb1","Feb2","Mar1","Mar2","Apr1"))
###  Remove spaces in .group
SamplePer$.group=gsub(" ", "", SamplePer$.group)
pd = position_dodge(0.4)
###  Plot

       aes(x     = SamplePer,
           y     = lsmean,
           label = .group)) +
  geom_point(shape  = 15,
             size   = 4,

messages.body_plain:
You can’t use both nudge and dodge.  The easiest way to get the vertical alignment you want is to use dodge.  So then you have to set the label height by passing a new y aesthetic.  If you also override the color aesthetic, you need to include a group aesthetic so that ggplot understands how to dodge the labels.

Here’s a MWE.

> library(ggplot2)
>
> ## Load data ----
> Plot_WaterDepth = read.csv('Plot_WaterDepth.csv')
> ## For solution 2, y position of the labels
> Plot_WaterDepth$label_y = Plot_WaterDepth$lsmean + 1
>
> ## Define underlying plot, w/out labels ----
> dodge = position_dodge(width = .5)
>
> basic_plot = ggplot(Plot_WaterDepth,

>        aes(x     = WaterDepth,
>            y     = lsmean,

>            group = PlotType,

>            color = PlotType,
>            label = .group)) +

>     geom_errorbar(aes(ymin  =  asymp.LCL,
>                       ymax  =  asymp.UCL),

>                   position = dodge)
>
> ## Solution 1 ----
> ## Labels at a fixed height
> basic_plot +
>     geom_text(aes(y = 4), color = 'black', position = dodge)
>
> ## Solution 2 ----
> ## Labels at variable height, relative to corresponding values
> basic_plot +
>     geom_text(aes(y = label_y), color = 'black', position = dodge)
>
----

messages.subject: PerMANOVA confidence intervals?
messages.subject_clean: PerMANOVA confidence intervals?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

This is more of a statistics question than an R question, but you all are so helpful I'm sure someone can point me in the right direction. I am working on a paper in which I compare community composition of two treatment groups using a Permutational Multivariate Analysis of Variance (PerMANOVA), with the "adonis" function in the "vegan" package. I presented the p-value of the PerMANOVA and a stacked bar graph of community composition. We recieved a review of the paper that says:

A notable omission is the reference to Figure 2, which discusses the PERMANOVA results but instead shows community composition bar graphs. I think it would be useful to show the modeled results with confidence limits to allow the reader to judge the the differences. This is a trivial implementation of a glm approach and would be more informative than the use of p-values, which in this case may not be appropriate and are almost certainly too restrictive in assessing the results of a field study.

I'm feeling pretty lost. The modeled results from the PerMANOVA involves a huge matrix of coefficients. I'm not sure how to get confidence intervals for each of the coefficients, and even if I did it would be a lot to take in (there are over 50 species in my community matrix). Does anyone know the "trivial implementation of the glm approach" that the reviewer refers to? I understood PerMANOVA to be useful in testing for overall differences between communities, not testing for individual differences in each taxon. Does anyone know more about PerMANOVA?

Thanks,
--
Rosemary Hartman
roseh...@gmail.com
301-538-0136
